verification.notes: First published March 2019 by Portfolio. Written from the author's experience leading design at a large social technology company; practitioner advice rather than research. All prose original.

title: An Elegant Puzzle
subtitle: Systems of Engineering Management
author: Will Larson
why_it_matters: It treats management as a systems problem with measurable stocks, flows and delays rather than a people-skills problem, which is why it survives contact with a real organisation. It remains the reference text for anyone running engineering teams at scale.

crux.headline: Manage the system, not the individual incidents
crux.body: Most management problems recur because they are produced by a structure rather than by the people caught inside it. Teams are the unit that matters, not individuals. Their size, their state of health, how work arrives and how debt accumulates all obey rules you can reason about. Once you see the org as a system with inputs, delays and feedback loops, the daily crises stop looking like separate emergencies and start looking like symptoms with a small number of underlying causes.

sparks.hook: Adding people to a struggling team usually makes it slower for months.
sparks.insight: The reflex when a team is drowning is to hire. But new people consume the capacity of the existing ones for a quarter or more before they contribute, so if the team is merely overloaded rather than genuinely under-resourced, hiring makes the next three months worse. What a stretched team usually needs is fewer things in flight, so it can finish something. What a permanently under-resourced team needs is people. Diagnosing which situation you are in is the whole decision.
sparks.why: Onboarding has a real, front-loaded cost paid by the people already there. That cost is invisible in a headcount plan, which is why hiring gets applied to problems it cannot solve.
sparks.apply: Before requesting headcount, cut your team's concurrent projects in half for six weeks and see whether throughput recovers on its own.

sparks.hook: Every team is in one of four states, and each needs a different fix.
sparks.insight: Teams are not simply good or bad. A team can be falling behind, where the backlog grows faster than it shrinks. It can be treading water, keeping the critical work alive but never getting ahead. It can be actively repaying accumulated debt. Or it can be innovating, with slack to spend on new things. Each state has one appropriate intervention and applying the wrong one wastes a quarter. You also cannot skip states: an overwhelmed team has to pass through the middle two before it can innovate.
sparks.why: The states form a sequence rather than a menu, which is why interventions that worked for one team fail for another that looks superficially similar but sits at a different point.
sparks.apply: Place each team you own into one of the four states this week, then apply only the matching intervention for the next quarter.

carousel.title: Falling behind: add people
carousel.body: The queue grows faster than the team can clear it and morale is dropping. This is the one situation where hiring genuinely is the answer, and it takes a quarter to land.

carousel.title: Treading water: cut the work
carousel.body: Critical things get done and nothing improves. Reduce concurrent projects hard so the team can finish something, because finishing is what creates the room to get ahead.

carousel.title: Repaying debt: add time
carousel.body: The team is fixing the foundations. Protect the schedule and resist the urge to inject new work; this stage looks unproductive from outside and is the one that pays for everything after it.

carousel.title: Innovating: leave them alone
carousel.body: There is slack, the backlog is short, and new work is being invented. Your job here is to defend the slack against the constant pressure to consume it.

sparks.hook: The team is the unit of work. Individuals are just where it happens.
sparks.insight: Organisations that assign projects to individuals get brittleness: knowledge concentrates in one head, the work stops when that person leaves, and nobody can take a holiday. Assigning ownership to teams instead is slower to feel productive and vastly more durable. It also changes how you plan. You stop trying to match a specific person to a specific task and start asking whether a team has a coherent area, enough people to sustain it, and a clear boundary with the teams next to it.
sparks.why: Team-level ownership survives turnover, illness and promotion; individual ownership does not. The cost is a short-term loss of the efficiency that comes from always using the best-matched person.
sparks.apply: List every critical system you own and name the team that owns it. Anything owned by a single person is a risk to be fixed this quarter.

sparks.hook: Teams below six are fragile. Above ten they need another manager.
sparks.insight: Team size is not a matter of taste. Below roughly six people, a team cannot sustain an on-call rotation, absorb a departure, or take a holiday without stalling, so it stays permanently anxious. Above roughly ten, a manager can no longer hold real context on each person's work and coordination overhead starts eating the gains from having more people. The band in between is where most teams work well, and drifting outside it produces problems that get misdiagnosed as culture or motivation.
sparks.why: Both limits come from concrete constraints: rotation coverage and resilience at the bottom, the manager's attention and communication paths at the top. Neither depends on how good the people are.
sparks.apply: Count the members of every team you own. Merge anything under five and split anything over ten, planning both moves this quarter.

sparks.hook: Migrations are the only way large systems ever pay down debt.
sparks.insight: Beyond a certain size, technical debt cannot be cleaned up incrementally, because the rate of new debt matches the rate you fix it. The only mechanism that changes the picture is a full migration: everything moves to the new approach and the old one is genuinely removed. Half-finished migrations are worse than none at all, because you now maintain two systems and every engineer must learn both. That means the deciding question is not whether the new approach is better but whether you will actually finish.
sparks.why: Partial migration leaves permanent duplicate cost, so the ability to complete matters more than the quality of the destination. Most organisations underestimate the tail of the work by a wide margin.
sparks.apply: List your unfinished migrations, pick the one closest to completion, and staff it until it is finished before starting anything new.

sparks.hook: Write policy for the common case and treat exceptions as exceptions.
sparks.insight: Managers make two opposite mistakes with rules. One is deciding everything case by case, which is exhausting, inconsistent and rewards whoever argues hardest. The other is writing a policy so comprehensive it covers every edge case and nobody can read it. The workable middle is a short policy that handles the ordinary situation well, plus an explicit route for exceptions that a named person approves. Exceptions handled openly are fine. Exceptions granted quietly are how a policy dies.
sparks.why: A policy exists to remove repeated decisions, so complexity defeats its own purpose. Making the exception path visible is what keeps the rule credible for everyone who did not get one.
sparks.apply: Take your most contested recurring decision, write a policy for the common case in under a page, and name who approves exceptions.

sparks.hook: You cannot mandate a change sideways. You can make it obvious.
sparks.insight: Most of the changes an engineering leader wants involve people they do not manage. Instructions do not work there, and neither does arguing in meetings. What does work is a sequence: build the thing yourself so it demonstrably exists, write down clearly how and why it works, and only then invite others to adopt it. Each step lowers the cost of the next person saying yes. Attempting the last step first is why so many good technical proposals die in a review committee.
sparks.why: Adoption without authority depends on lowering risk for the adopter. A working example plus documentation removes most of that risk; a proposal document alone removes none of it.
sparks.apply: Pick one change you have been arguing for, stop arguing, build a working version in one team, and write up what happened.

carousel.title: Build it somewhere real
carousel.body: Implement the change in one team, ideally your own, and run it long enough to hit the problems. A working example ends most of the theoretical objections by itself.

carousel.title: Write down what happened
carousel.body: Document the approach, the results and the parts that went badly. Including the failures is what makes the write-up credible to people who did not choose this.

carousel.title: Make adoption cheap
carousel.body: Provide the templates, tooling or migration script so the next team spends hours rather than weeks. Adoption cost is usually the real objection behind a stated one.

carousel.title: Let it spread, then standardise
carousel.body: Once several teams have chosen it, make it the default. Standardising before there is evidence turns a good idea into an imposed one people work around.

sparks.hook: A career ladder is mostly a device for reducing arguments about promotion.
sparks.insight: Without written levels, promotion decisions get made on visibility, advocacy and who is closest to a decision-maker, and everyone can feel it even when nobody can prove it. A ladder that describes observable behaviour at each level does not remove judgement, but it moves the argument to a shared document instead of a private one. It also makes the manager's job easier: instead of defending a decision, you point at the gap between what somebody does and what the next level describes.
sparks.why: Legible criteria reduce the influence of proximity and self-promotion on advancement. The ladder is imperfect and gameable; the undocumented alternative is worse and less fair.
sparks.apply: Write one paragraph of observable behaviour for each level on your team, share it, and use it in your next promotion discussion.

sparks.hook: Interviewing is expensive engineering time nobody puts on the plan.
sparks.insight: Every interview loop consumes several hours from people who were otherwise building things, plus the recovery time around it. Organisations rarely count this, so they run wasteful processes and then wonder why delivery slipped during a hiring push. Counting it changes decisions: you shorten loops, you stop interviewing for roles you are not going to fill, and you concentrate interviewing among people who are good at it rather than spreading it evenly as a tax on everyone.
sparks.why: Unmeasured costs are always overspent. Making interview hours visible turns hiring into a resourcing decision rather than an invisible drain on the same teams under delivery pressure.
sparks.apply: Total your team's interview hours for last month, put the number in your capacity plan, and cut one stage from the loop.

sparks.hook: Do the work that only you can do. Give away the rest, even the fun parts.
sparks.insight: Every manager has a set of tasks that they alone can perform: the organisational decisions, the conversations that require your authority, the strategy nobody else has the context to write. Around that sits a much larger set of work you happen to be good at and enjoy. Holding onto the second set is understandable, since it is where you feel competent, and it is also what stops your team growing. The test is not whether you do it well. It is whether anyone else could.
sparks.why: Doing work others could do has a hidden cost: it removes their development opportunity and occupies the time your unique work needed. Both costs land later, which is why the trade feels free now.
sparks.apply: List everything you did last week, mark each as only-you or someone-else, and hand over the largest someone-else item this month.

actions: Place every team you own into one of the four states and apply only the matching intervention for a full quarter.
Count your unfinished migrations, staff the one closest to completion until it is genuinely done, and start nothing new until then.
Write a one-page policy for your most contested recurring decision and name the person who approves exceptions to it.
Add your team's monthly interview hours to the capacity plan, then remove one stage from the hiring loop.
not_for_you_if: You do not lead engineers or you want narrative and encouragement rather than dense operational advice organised as a reference.

verification.notes: First published 2019 by Stripe Press. Practitioner writing drawn from the author's experience leading infrastructure and engineering organisations; the numeric team-size bands are heuristics rather than measured thresholds.

title: Turn the Ship Around!
subtitle: A True Story of Turning Followers into Leaders
author: L. David Marquet
why_it_matters: It is the clearest account of how to move decision-making authority downward without losing control, written by a submarine captain who had to do it because he did not know his own ship's systems well enough to give the usual orders.

crux.headline: Move the authority to where the information already is
crux.body: The standard model puts decisions at the top and information at the bottom, then spends enormous effort moving information upward. Reversing it works better: push the authority down to the people who can already see the problem. That only holds if two other things rise with it. People need the technical competence to decide well, and they need to understand the goal clearly enough to decide in the right direction. Authority without either produces chaos, which is why most attempts fail.

sparks.hook: The better your orders are, the worse your crew gets at thinking.
sparks.insight: A capable leader who gives clear, correct instructions produces a team that executes well and cannot function without them. Everyone waits, because waiting has always been rewarded and initiative has occasionally been punished. The organisation looks excellent while the leader is present and collapses when they leave, which is usually treated as evidence of how good the leader was. It is better read as evidence of what they built: a system with a single point of failure sitting in the chair.
sparks.why: Competence at the top suppresses initiative below it, because deferring is always the lower-risk choice for the individual. The effect is invisible until the leader is absent.
sparks.apply: Go a full day without answering a question with an instruction. Ask what they think should happen and agree with it unless it is genuinely unsafe.

sparks.hook: Change the language from asking permission to stating an intention.
sparks.insight: How people phrase things determines how much thinking they do. Someone who asks what they should do has handed you the problem and stopped working on it. Someone who tells you what they are about to do, and why, has already done the analysis and is giving you a chance to intervene. The change is small and the effect is not: you now hear their reasoning rather than their question, and correcting a plan is far cheaper than generating one for them.
sparks.why: Requesting permission transfers ownership upward; announcing intent keeps it in place while preserving your ability to stop something. The person also has to think it through before speaking.
sparks.apply: Tell your team to bring you intentions rather than questions this month, and respond to each with agreement or one clarifying question.

carousel.title: Ban the permission question
carousel.body: Say explicitly that you no longer want to be asked what to do. The habit is deep and will not change on hints, so name the new expectation out loud.

carousel.title: Require the reasoning
carousel.body: Ask people to say what they intend and the two or three reasons behind it. The reasoning is the part you actually need in order to judge quickly.

carousel.title: Say yes far more than feels safe
carousel.body: If the plan is defensible and reversible, agree even when you would have chosen differently. Overriding good-enough decisions is how the old habit returns.

carousel.title: Debrief the misses together
carousel.body: When an intention turns out badly, work through the reasoning rather than the outcome. Punishing the result teaches people to go back to asking you.

sparks.hook: Handing over authority to people who lack competence is abandonment.
sparks.insight: Empowerment fails most often because only one of the three necessary things was changed. Giving people authority without also raising their technical skill produces confident bad decisions, and everybody concludes that delegation does not work here. Authority has to move down at the same pace that competence moves up. That means a real, deliberate investment in training, and accepting that the transfer of decisions happens over quarters rather than in an announcement at an all-hands.
sparks.why: Authority, competence and clarity of purpose are interdependent. Raising one alone reliably produces a failure that gets blamed on the idea rather than on the incomplete implementation.
sparks.apply: For one decision you want to delegate, write what the person must know to make it well, then teach that before handing it over.

sparks.hook: People cannot decide in the right direction without knowing the destination.
sparks.insight: The third condition for pushing decisions down is that everyone understands what the organisation is actually trying to achieve, in enough detail to apply it to a situation nobody anticipated. Most teams have a stated goal that is too abstract to guide a real trade-off. If someone has to choose between speed and safety at two in the morning, a slogan gives them nothing. What they need is to have heard you make similar trade-offs out loud, repeatedly, until they can predict your reasoning.
sparks.why: Judgement transfers through worked examples rather than through statements of principle. People learn what you prioritise by watching you decide, which is why reasoning has to be spoken.
sparks.apply: Narrate your reasoning out loud for the next three decisions you make, including the option you rejected and why you rejected it.

sparks.hook: Say what you are thinking before you are sure. It spreads context fast.
sparks.insight: Leaders usually stay quiet until they have a conclusion, which looks decisive and starves everyone of context. Speaking your uncertainty aloud — what you are noticing, what is bothering you, what you are unsure about — gives the people around you the raw material to think with. It also legitimises doing the same thing back. In a high-stakes environment this is how a team catches a problem early: somebody voices a half-formed worry and another person recognises what it is.
sparks.why: Half-formed observations carry information that finished conclusions have already discarded. Making them speakable is what lets a group notice a problem before it becomes an event.
sparks.apply: In your next team meeting, say one thing you are uncertain about before you have resolved it, and ask whether anyone shares the worry.

sparks.hook: Do not brief people before a job. Have them tell you the plan.
sparks.insight: A briefing lets everybody nod while thinking about something else, and then you discover at the point of failure that half the room was not listening. Inverting it changes everything: instead of telling the team the plan, you ask them questions about it and they demonstrate that they know. The person running the job has to have prepared, and any gap in understanding surfaces beforehand rather than during. It takes the same amount of time and produces a completely different level of readiness.
sparks.why: Passive listening does not reveal comprehension gaps, while active recall does. Requiring people to state the plan converts a compliance ritual into an actual check.
sparks.apply: Replace your next project kick-off briefing with a session where the team explains the plan and the risks back to you.

carousel.title: Send the material ahead
carousel.body: Circulate whatever people need to read beforehand and say plainly that the session assumes they have read it. Reading aloud in the room is what makes briefings useless.

carousel.title: Ask, do not tell
carousel.body: Open by asking the person running the work to walk through what happens, step by step. Your job in this session is questions, not statements.

carousel.title: Probe the failure points
carousel.body: Ask what they do if the first step goes wrong, who they call, and what the fallback is. Gaps surface here at almost no cost, which is the whole point.

carousel.title: Decide whether to proceed
carousel.body: If the answers are vague, delay rather than hoping. A session that can never result in a postponement is a ritual rather than a check.

sparks.hook: Most errors are not ignorance. They are automatic hands moving too fast.
sparks.insight: In practised environments, mistakes rarely come from not knowing. They come from doing the familiar action without attention, on the wrong valve, the wrong record, the wrong account. The counter is a deliberate pause before a consequential action: slow down, say aloud what you are about to do, and let anyone nearby object. It looks slightly theatrical and it works, because it converts an automatic motion into a conscious one and gives other people a window to catch it.
sparks.why: Skilled routine actions bypass deliberate checking, which is exactly what makes them fast and what makes them go wrong. Vocalising re-engages attention and adds a second observer.
sparks.apply: Define the three actions on your team that cannot be undone, and require saying them out loud to another person before executing.

sparks.hook: Watch for the moment your team stops thinking and starts complying.
sparks.insight: The failure has a specific signature and you can learn to spot it. People stop bringing alternatives. Meetings end with agreement that arrived too quickly. Somebody says they were only following the process, and they are right. Each is a signal that the environment has taught people that judgement is riskier than obedience. Because the work still gets done, the problem is easy to miss until something unusual happens and nobody adjusts, because adjusting was never permitted.
sparks.why: Compliance produces adequate results in normal conditions and fails badly in novel ones. That is why the cost only appears at the moment you most need people to think.
sparks.apply: Ask three people this week to tell you something they disagreed with and did anyway, and change one of those decisions.

sparks.hook: Short conversations early prevent long ones later.
sparks.insight: When a leader is unavailable, everything gets saved for a formal review, which means work travels a long way in the wrong direction before anyone checks. Frequent thirty-second conversations at the start of a task cost almost nothing and catch the misunderstanding while it is still cheap. The instinct to protect your calendar from small interruptions is understandable and it exports a much larger cost: whole weeks of work built on an assumption you could have corrected in half a minute.
sparks.why: The cost of correcting a direction rises steeply with elapsed time and work invested. Early, cheap conversations are the highest-return use of a manager's attention.
sparks.apply: Make yourself interruptible for thirty seconds at any time this week, and measure how many misunderstandings you catch before they cost anything.

sparks.hook: One ship, one captain, one outcome. Treat it as a case, not a proof.
sparks.insight: The evidence here is a single vessel that went from a poor ranking to a strong one after a deliberate change in how decisions were made, plus an unusual number of its officers being promoted afterwards. That is genuinely striking and it is still one case, reported by the person who led it, in an environment with extreme selection, training and shared standards. Take the mechanism seriously and be careful about the scale of the claim. Your organisation lacks the training pipeline that made the transfer of authority survivable.
sparks.why: A single self-reported case cannot separate the intervention from the leader, the crew or the moment. The underlying logic is sound and widely echoed; the magnitude of the result is not transferable.
sparks.apply: Before copying the approach, write down what your organisation lacks that the ship had, and build that first.

actions: Tell your team to bring you intentions rather than questions for one month, and agree with every defensible, reversible plan they bring.
Pick one decision you want to delegate, write what the person needs to know to make it well, and teach that before transferring it.
Replace your next kick-off briefing with a session where the team explains the plan and its risks back to you.
Narrate your reasoning out loud for three decisions this week, including the option you rejected and the reason you rejected it.
not_for_you_if: Military settings put you off, or you need evidence beyond one commander's account of one unusually well-trained organisation.

verification.notes: Originally self-published in 2012 and reissued by Portfolio in 2013. A first-person account of commanding a US Navy submarine; the sparks flag the single-case limitation explicitly.

title: Extreme Ownership
subtitle: How U.S. Navy SEALs Lead and Win
author: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin
why_it_matters: It made total accountability a usable operating stance rather than a slogan, and it is unusually clear about the practical mechanics of planning, prioritising under pressure and getting a team to act without waiting for instructions.

crux.headline: If it happened in your area, it is yours to own
crux.body: The most useful thing a leader can do with a failure is refuse every available excuse. Not because the excuses are false — the brief really was unclear, the other team really did miss the deadline — but because as long as the cause sits outside you, there is nothing you can change. Taking ownership of everything in your area, including the parts you did not cause, is what converts a complaint into a problem you can actually work on. It is a stance chosen for its usefulness.

sparks.hook: The moment you find someone else to blame, you stop being able to fix it.
sparks.insight: Blame is usually accurate and always useless. When a project fails, there genuinely are contributing causes outside your control, and cataloguing them changes nothing about your next attempt. Taking ownership of the whole outcome is a deliberate move that hands you the only lever you have. It also propagates: a team whose leader visibly absorbs the failure stops constructing defences, and starts spending that energy on the actual problem. Nobody below you will own anything you refuse to own first.
sparks.why: The stance is chosen for its effects rather than its accuracy. Attributing failure externally is psychologically comfortable and removes every route to improvement, which is why capable teams treat it as a warning sign.
sparks.apply: Take the last thing that went wrong and write down your contribution to it, without a single sentence about anybody else.

sparks.hook: Swap the leaders between a failing team and a winning one, and watch.
sparks.insight: The claim is that performance follows leadership more than it follows the composition of a team, illustrated by boat crews in selection training where moving the leaders moved the results. It is a memorable demonstration and it is one anecdote from a highly unusual environment, so hold it loosely. What is more defensible is the practical version: before concluding you have a weak team, check what the person leading it is doing, because that is the variable you can change fastest and it is the one nobody examines.
sparks.why: This rests on a single training anecdote rather than a controlled comparison, and selection environments are unlike workplaces. The weaker version — check leadership before blaming the team — survives the scrutiny.
sparks.apply: Take your lowest-performing team and spend a week observing how it is led before you make any change to who is on it.

sparks.hook: If you cannot explain why, do not pass the instruction down.
sparks.insight: Managers routinely relay decisions they do not understand, and the team hears the uncertainty regardless of the words. The alternative is to go back up and ask until you can explain the reasoning in your own words. Sometimes you will discover the decision is worse than you thought and you have a case to make. Usually you will find a rationale nobody bothered to communicate. Either way, relaying an order you cannot justify teaches your team that reasons are optional here.
sparks.why: A leader's visible conviction is a large part of what makes a decision executable. Passing along an instruction while privately disagreeing produces compliance without effort, which looks like agreement and performs like resistance.
sparks.apply: Before relaying the next decision from above, write the reason in your own words. If you cannot, go back and ask before you announce it.

sparks.hook: If the newest person cannot repeat the plan, the plan is too complicated.
sparks.insight: Complex plans fail under pressure because pressure removes the capacity to hold them. The test is simple and slightly humiliating: ask the most junior person to explain what happens and what they do if the first step goes wrong. If the answer is vague, the problem is not their attention. It is that you have built something that only works while everyone is calm, well-briefed and reading from the document. Simplicity is not a lack of ambition; it is what allows an ambitious plan to survive contact with a bad day.
sparks.why: Cognitive load rises sharply under stress, so plan complexity that is manageable in a planning room becomes unmanageable in execution. The junior-person test is a cheap proxy for that threshold.
sparks.apply: Have the most junior person on your team explain the current plan back to you, and simplify everything they could not state clearly.

carousel.title: State the goal in one line
carousel.body: Write what success looks like in a single sentence anyone could repeat. If it takes a paragraph, nobody will be holding it when things get difficult.

carousel.title: Build the plan with the team
carousel.body: Have the people doing the work construct the steps rather than receiving them. Understanding comes from building it, and they will spot what you could not.

carousel.title: Plan for the likely failure
carousel.body: Name the two or three things most likely to go wrong and decide the response now. Contingencies invented under pressure are worse and slower than ones chosen calmly.

carousel.title: Test it on the newest person
carousel.body: Ask the most junior member to explain the plan and what they would do if step one failed. Whatever they cannot state clearly is what you simplify.

sparks.hook: When everything is urgent, say the top priority out loud and start there.
sparks.insight: Under pressure the instinct is to try to hold every problem at once, which produces paralysis dressed up as busyness. The alternative is mechanical: step back, name the single highest priority out loud so the whole team hears the same thing, direct effort onto it, and then re-evaluate rather than assuming the ranking still holds. Saying it aloud is the part people skip, and it is what stops each person privately picking a different top problem and working against each other.
sparks.why: Sequential focus outperforms parallel attention when problems are interdependent, and stating the priority publicly is what synchronises the team's effort rather than fragmenting it.
sparks.apply: Next time your team faces three crises at once, say which one comes first out loud, then check the ranking again in an hour.

carousel.title: Step back from it
carousel.body: Physically or mentally detach for a minute. You cannot rank problems while inside one of them, and the pull to keep reacting is what produces the paralysis.

carousel.title: Name the top one aloud
carousel.body: Say which problem is first, clearly enough that everybody heard the same sentence. Unspoken priorities let each person choose a different one and work in opposite directions.

carousel.title: Point everything at it
carousel.body: Move the people and attention onto that single problem, including your own. Holding a reserve back for the other crises is how none of them get solved.

carousel.title: Re-rank, out loud again
carousel.body: Once it is contained, restate the new top priority rather than assuming everyone updated. Priorities decay quickly and stale ones are worse than none.

sparks.hook: Teams that compete internally are just losing to the outside more slowly.
sparks.insight: Departments given separate targets will optimise against each other, and each of them will be behaving rationally. Sales blames delivery, delivery blames sales, and both are partly right. The fix has to come from the leaders: treat the other team's problem as your problem, share information before you are asked, and refuse to score points off a peer even when they are clearly at fault. That is slow to establish and it is the only thing that makes cross-functional work faster than it is adversarial.
sparks.why: Internal competition is generated by structure and measurement rather than by personality, so it cannot be fixed by asking people to cooperate more. It requires leaders to absorb the cost of going first.
sparks.apply: Pick the team you most often blame, ask their leader what you are doing that makes their job harder, and fix one thing.

sparks.hook: You cannot lead a team through a decision they have never seen you make.
sparks.insight: Decentralised action requires people to know what you would do without asking you, and that knowledge does not come from a briefing. It comes from having been present while you weighed a similar call, heard what you discarded, and watched the outcome. Which means the way to build a team that acts without you is to make your reasoning visible now, repeatedly, on decisions that do not matter much, so that the pattern is available when a decision that matters arrives and you are unreachable.
sparks.why: Independent judgement is learned by pattern-matching against observed examples. A stated set of principles is far too coarse to resolve a real trade-off in the moment.
sparks.apply: Pick a small decision each week and make it in front of your team, saying what you weighed and what you decided against.

sparks.hook: Structure is not the opposite of freedom. It is what pays for it.
sparks.insight: Autonomy without agreed standards produces a team that has to renegotiate everything, and renegotiation is where the time goes. Fixed routines — the same daily rhythm, the same format for a handover, the same checks before a release — remove decisions that were never worth making and leave attention for the ones that are. The paradox is real: teams with the most rigid basics are usually the ones able to improvise successfully, because improvisation is expensive and they have saved their capacity for it.
sparks.why: Routine reduces the cognitive cost of ordinary work, freeing capacity for the novel parts. Teams with no fixed structure spend that capacity on coordination instead.
sparks.apply: Standardise one recurring thing on your team this week — a handover format, a daily rhythm, a release check — and leave it fixed for a quarter.

sparks.hook: Managing your own boss is part of the job, not a complaint about it.
sparks.insight: When your manager is not giving you what you need, the useful assumption is that they lack information rather than judgement. That makes it your task to supply it: what you are doing, what is blocking you, what you need decided and by when. Most leaders wait to be asked and then resent the outcome. Presenting a clear recommendation with the reasoning attached is far more likely to move a decision than a complaint, and it is one of the few ways to gain influence you were not formally given.
sparks.why: Senior decisions are usually made with less context than people below assume. Supplying that context is the highest-leverage available move for anyone without formal authority.
sparks.apply: Send your manager a short note this week with one blocked decision, your recommendation, and the date you need an answer.

sparks.hook: Every leadership strength has a failure mode sitting right beside it.
sparks.insight: Decisiveness becomes recklessness. Confidence becomes an inability to hear a correction. Caring about people becomes an unwillingness to hold them to anything. Being demanding becomes contempt. There is no setting that is safe, which means the skill is not choosing the right qualities but continuously noticing which way you are currently drifting. Most leaders have one habitual direction of drift, and the people around them can name it instantly if you make it safe to say.
sparks.why: Leadership qualities are not virtues with fixed values but positions on a scale with a bad end at either extreme. The useful question is which end you personally drift towards under pressure.
sparks.apply: Ask two people which direction you overcorrect in under pressure, and put a check in place for that specific tendency.

actions: Write your own contribution to the last failure in your area, with no sentence about anybody else's part in it.
Have the most junior person explain your current plan back to you, and simplify everything they could not state clearly.
Ask the leader of the team you most often blame what you do that makes their job harder, then fix one thing.
Make one small decision in front of your team each week, saying aloud what you weighed and what you decided against.
not_for_you_if: Combat framing puts you off, or you want evidence rather than war stories and consulting cases drawn from the authors' own clients.

verification.notes: First published October 2015 by St Martin's Press. Combat accounts paired with business cases from the authors' own consultancy, so the business evidence is self-selected; this limitation is flagged in the sparks.

title: Team of Teams
subtitle: New Rules of Engagement for a Complex World
author: Stanley McChrystal with Tantum Collins, David Silverman and Chris Fussell
why_it_matters: It explains why organisations built for efficiency fail against fast, networked opponents, and what a large hierarchy has to give up to become adaptable. The argument that information sharing must come before pushing decisions down has reshaped how large institutions think about structure.

crux.headline: Optimised organisations break in unpredictable environments
crux.body: A century of management aimed at efficiency: break work into parts, specialise, remove waste, and route decisions upward. That works when the environment is stable enough to plan against. When conditions change faster than information can climb the hierarchy, the same design becomes the weakness. What replaces it is a network of small teams that each hold the whole picture, connected well enough that they can act without waiting, with the leader maintaining conditions rather than issuing moves.

sparks.hook: Being efficient and being adaptable are usually opposite decisions.
sparks.insight: Efficiency comes from removing slack, standardising, and eliminating duplication. Adaptability comes from having spare capacity, multiple people who understand the same thing, and room to try something that might not work. You cannot maximise both, and most organisations optimise for efficiency by default because it is the one you can measure this quarter. The cost only appears when something unexpected happens and there is nobody with the spare attention or overlapping knowledge to respond.
sparks.why: The trade-off is structural, not a matter of effort. Redundancy looks like waste on any efficiency measure, which is why it gets removed in good times and missed badly in bad ones.
sparks.apply: Name one place where you have removed all slack for efficiency, and deliberately restore some of it before you need it.

sparks.hook: Complicated problems can be solved. Complex ones can only be adapted to.
sparks.insight: A complicated system has many parts and predictable behaviour: an engine, a payroll process, a supply chain in normal conditions. Study it hard enough and you can forecast it. A complex system has interacting parts whose combined behaviour cannot be derived from the pieces, which is why weather, markets and insurgencies resist prediction no matter how much data you gather. Treating a complex situation as merely complicated leads to more analysis, more planning and more surprise, which is the reliable signature of the mistake.
sparks.why: The distinction changes what a good response looks like. For complicated problems you invest in prediction; for complex ones prediction is wasted effort and the investment goes into speed of response.
sparks.apply: Sort your current major risks into predictable and unpredictable, and stop building detailed forecasts for anything in the second column.

sparks.hook: A small team works brilliantly. Twenty of them together usually do not.
sparks.insight: Everyone knows how a good small team behaves: people trust each other, information moves without process, anyone can raise anything. The problem is that those properties stop at the team boundary. Put twenty excellent teams in one organisation and they will compete, hoard information and optimise locally, because each has become a tribe with its own interests. Scaling is not about making bigger teams. It is about recreating between teams the relationships that already exist inside them.
sparks.why: Trust and shared context degrade sharply across group boundaries, so the properties that make a small team effective do not aggregate. They have to be deliberately rebuilt at the seams.
sparks.apply: Identify the two teams whose poor coordination costs you the most, and create one shared forum they both attend weekly.

sparks.hook: Share context first. Push down decisions second. Reversing that order fails.
sparks.insight: Empowerment programmes usually announce that people can now decide for themselves, and then produce worse decisions, because those people cannot see enough of the picture to decide well. The order matters. First you make the whole situation genuinely visible to everybody, including the parts that used to be restricted. Only once people can see what you can see does handing them authority produce anything good. Doing the second without the first is what gives delegation its bad reputation.
sparks.why: Decision quality depends on context, and pushing authority to people without it converts good intentions into fast mistakes. Sequencing is the single most transferable lesson here.
sparks.apply: Before delegating a class of decision, list what you know that they do not, and make all of it routinely available first.

carousel.title: Open the information
carousel.body: Default to sharing rather than restricting. Most of what an organisation protects is protected out of habit, and the cost of that habit is decisions made blind.

carousel.title: Build one shared forum
carousel.body: Create a regular session where every part of the organisation reports what it sees, and where anyone can listen. Attendance across boundaries is the point, not the reporting.

carousel.title: Make leaders answer in public
carousel.body: Have senior people ask and answer questions in that forum. It signals that the information is genuinely shared and stops the real conversation moving elsewhere.

carousel.title: Then move the authority
carousel.body: Once people demonstrably see the whole picture, push decisions to them and hold the line when the first one goes badly. Pulling authority back at the first error ends the experiment.

sparks.hook: A slower decision made close to the problem beats a fast one made far away.
sparks.insight: Beyond a certain speed of change, the time a decision spends travelling up and back down costs more than the quality it gains from being made by someone senior. A good enough decision now beats an excellent one after the situation has moved. This is uncomfortable because it means accepting worse individual decisions in exchange for a faster overall system, and the bad ones are visible while the delay you avoided is not.
sparks.why: Decision latency is a real cost that rarely appears on anyone's report, while a poor decision made locally is highly visible. That asymmetry is why organisations centralise even when it is hurting them.
sparks.apply: Measure how long your last five significant decisions took from question to answer, then push the fastest-decaying category downward.

sparks.hook: Stop playing chess with your organisation and start growing conditions.
sparks.insight: The heroic model of leadership is someone who sees the whole board and moves the pieces. In a fast-moving environment that person becomes the bottleneck, and their main contribution is delay. The alternative role is less satisfying and more useful: maintain the conditions under which good decisions happen without you. That means keeping information flowing, keeping the goal clear, protecting people who acted sensibly and got a bad outcome, and resisting the urge to take back control every time something goes wrong.
sparks.why: As decisions distribute, the leader's leverage moves from making calls to shaping the environment. The difficulty is that the new role produces almost no visible evidence of your own contribution.
sparks.apply: For one week, make no decision that somebody closer to the problem could have made, and spend that time removing their blockers.

sparks.hook: Restricting information to those who need it guarantees nobody sees the whole.
sparks.insight: Sharing information only with people who obviously need it sounds prudent and quietly destroys an organisation's ability to notice things. The person who spots that two unrelated reports describe the same underlying problem is almost never the person either report was addressed to. Restricting by default removes exactly those accidental connections. The honest trade is that broad sharing carries real risk of leaks and noise, and in most organisations that risk is much smaller than the cost of everyone working half-blind.
sparks.why: Insight often comes from unexpected combinations, which need-to-know rules make structurally impossible. The security benefit is real but usually smaller than the coordination cost it creates.
sparks.apply: Pick one report currently restricted by habit rather than by regulation, and share it with everyone for a quarter.

sparks.hook: Send your best people to sit inside the team you cooperate with worst.
sparks.insight: Cross-team relationships built through process documents do not survive pressure. Relationships built by an actual person who spent months embedded in the other team do. Sending somebody good, for a long enough period that they build real trust, is expensive and it is the most reliable way to connect two groups that keep failing each other. The reason it works is that coordination problems are almost always trust problems wearing a process costume.
sparks.why: Trust between groups is carried by individuals rather than by agreements. An embedded person creates a route for information that no interface document ever produces.
sparks.apply: Choose the boundary that fails most often and place one respected person inside the other team for at least three months.

sparks.hook: You cannot plan your way out of a situation that changes weekly.
sparks.insight: Detailed long-range plans are comforting and they are a bet that the future resembles the assumptions you made when you wrote them. In a volatile environment those assumptions decay within weeks, but the plan continues to direct effort long after it stopped describing reality. The alternative is not the absence of planning. It is shorter cycles, a clearly stated intent that survives changing details, and a genuine willingness to abandon the plan when the situation says something different.
sparks.why: Plans have a half-life determined by how fast the environment moves. Continuing to execute a decayed plan is a common and expensive failure because abandoning it looks like indecision.
sparks.apply: Cut your planning horizon in half, and write down the two assumptions that would invalidate the plan if they changed.

carousel.title: Write the intent, not the steps
carousel.body: State what outcome matters and why, in language that still applies when the details change. Steps expire quickly; a clearly expressed purpose survives most surprises.

carousel.title: Shorten the cycle
carousel.body: Replace the annual plan with a shorter loop that ends in a real decision. The point is not speed for its own sake but making the plan cheap enough to discard.

carousel.title: Name the fragile assumptions
carousel.body: Write the two or three beliefs the plan depends on. When one visibly breaks, that is your trigger to replan rather than a reason to work harder at the old one.

carousel.title: Say when you abandoned it
carousel.body: When you drop a plan, announce it and explain why. Silent abandonment teaches people that plans are theatre and nothing said in them needs to be taken seriously.

sparks.hook: One organisation, one war, one commander telling the story afterwards.
sparks.insight: The account here is a single military organisation with extraordinary resources, selection and training, restructured under enormous pressure, described by the person who led it. Operational tempo clearly increased. Whether the strategic outcome justified any of it is genuinely contested, and none of that is separable from the specific people and moment involved. The structural argument stands well on its own logic and on the wider literature about networks. Treat the case as illustration rather than as demonstration of what will happen to you.
sparks.why: Self-reported organisational turnarounds have no control group and strong incentives towards a tidy narrative. The underlying claims about information flow and decision latency have independent support; the scale of the result does not.
sparks.apply: Before importing the model, write down which conditions your organisation lacks — shared training, common language, real urgency — and build those first.

actions: Open one information source currently restricted by habit rather than regulation, and share it with the whole organisation for a quarter.
Create a regular forum where every team reports what it sees and anyone may attend, and have senior people answer questions in it.
Place one respected person inside the team you coordinate with worst, for at least three months, with no deliverable but relationships.
Halve your planning horizon and write down the two assumptions whose failure would trigger a replan.
not_for_you_if: You lead a small team in a stable environment, or you want organisational research rather than a commander's account of one campaign.

verification.notes: First published May 2015 by Portfolio, co-written with Tantum Collins, David Silverman and Chris Fussell. The strategic outcome of the campaign described is contested; the sparks say so explicitly.

title: The Culture Code
subtitle: The Secrets of Highly Successful Groups
author: Daniel Coyle
why_it_matters: It treats culture as a set of observable signals people send each other rather than a set of stated values, which makes it something a manager can actually change on a Tuesday. It is also the most readable route into the research on psychological safety.

crux.headline: Culture is signals people send, not values on a wall
crux.body: Groups do not run on their stated beliefs. They run on thousands of small signals that tell each member whether they are safe here, whether it is acceptable to admit a problem, and whether the work means anything. Those signals are concrete: who gets interrupted, what happens when somebody is wrong, whether the leader ever admits ignorance. Change the signals and behaviour follows. Change the poster and nothing does.

sparks.hook: One negative person changes a whole group's output. So does one who counters it.
sparks.insight: In a well-known set of experiments, an actor was placed inside working groups playing a disruptive role — slacking, sniping, or draining energy — and the groups performed markedly worse regardless of how capable their members were. What is more useful is the exception. When one person in the group responded by asking questions, warming the room and drawing others back in, the effect largely disappeared. A single individual can set the emotional temperature, in either direction, and it does not have to be the manager.
sparks.why: This comes from real experimental work on group dynamics rather than anecdote, which is unusual for culture writing. The size of the effect in a lab task should still be held more loosely than the direction of it.
sparks.apply: Identify who currently sets your team's emotional temperature, and either coach them or make sure somebody else is deliberately countering it.

sparks.hook: Children beat business students at the same task, repeatedly.
sparks.insight: Given a building challenge with spaghetti and tape, groups of young children routinely outperform groups of business school students. The children do not strategise, they just try something, watch it fall, and try again. The students spend most of the time working out who is in charge and what the socially correct suggestion is, then build one careful structure that fails with no time left. The lesson is not that expertise is useless. It is that status negotiation consumes an enormous amount of the effort a group thinks it is spending on the problem.
sparks.why: This is a widely repeated workshop exercise rather than a controlled study, so treat it as a vivid illustration. The underlying point about status jostling crowding out iteration is well supported elsewhere.
sparks.apply: In your next group task, ban discussion for the first ten minutes and require a rough working attempt before anyone proposes an approach.

sparks.hook: Belonging is transmitted in signals so small nobody consciously registers them.
sparks.insight: People decide whether they are safe in a group from evidence that is almost invisible: whether someone turns towards them when they speak, how the conversation is distributed, whether they are physically close, whether they are interrupted. None of this is deliberate and all of it is being read continuously. That is why a team can feel cold despite everyone being polite, and why sending an email about inclusion changes nothing. The signals have to change, and the leader sends more of them than anyone else.
sparks.why: Humans read social inclusion continuously and largely below awareness, which is why the felt experience of a team so often contradicts its stated norms. Small behaviours dominate because they are frequent.
sparks.apply: In your next meeting, count who spoke and for how long, then directly invite the two quietest people into the next one.

sparks.hook: Admitting you got it wrong is the cheapest culture change available.
sparks.insight: A team's willingness to surface problems is set almost entirely by what the most senior person does with their own errors. Say clearly that you were wrong, without softening it into a learning opportunity, and you have demonstrated that the cost is survivable. Everyone in the room recalculates. The move has to be specific and slightly uncomfortable — a real mistake with a real consequence — because a carefully chosen trivial one reads as performance and teaches the opposite lesson.
sparks.why: People calibrate the risk of admitting error by watching the highest-status person, since they have the most to lose. That makes the leader's admission disproportionately informative to everyone else.
sparks.apply: Name one real mistake you made this month in your next team meeting, say what it cost, and do not attach a silver lining.

sparks.hook: Cooperation starts when somebody admits they need help, and gets it.
sparks.insight: Groups become cooperative through a repeated exchange rather than through good intentions. One person signals a genuine need — I do not understand this, I am stuck, I got this wrong — and another responds without cost or judgement. Both are now slightly more exposed and slightly more connected, and the next request is easier. The loop is fragile at the start: one dismissive response closes it for months. Which is why the first few exchanges should involve you, and why your response matters more than your invitation.
sparks.why: Cooperation is built by demonstrated safety rather than declared openness. The loop only starts if the first response is warm, which is why the leader has to be involved early.
sparks.apply: Ask one person for help this week with something you genuinely cannot do, and thank them specifically in front of others.

carousel.title: Go first yourself
carousel.body: Admit a real gap in front of the team. Asking others to be open while remaining polished yourself is the most common way this fails before it starts.

carousel.title: Respond warmly, every time
carousel.body: When somebody admits a problem, your first reaction sets the price for everyone watching. Curiosity and thanks; never surprise, correction or a raised eyebrow.

carousel.title: Ask the second question
carousel.body: Do not accept the first answer to what is going wrong. The useful information sits behind a follow-up question and a pause you did not fill.

carousel.title: Repeat until it is normal
carousel.body: One exchange proves nothing. The loop becomes a norm when it has survived several rounds, including one where the admission was genuinely costly.

sparks.hook: Say why the work matters far more often than feels reasonable.
sparks.insight: Leaders stop repeating the purpose long before their teams stop needing it, because they hear it in their own head constantly and assume everyone else does too. Groups with strong shared purpose tend to be almost tedious about it: the same story, the same reason, the same reminder of who this is for, embedded in ordinary conversations rather than saved for a quarterly presentation. Repetition is not a failure of imagination. It is what makes a purpose available to somebody at the moment they have to make a trade-off.
sparks.why: Message decay is fast and uneven, so a purpose stated once reaches almost nobody in a usable form. Frequency is what puts it within reach at the moment of a decision.
sparks.apply: Attach one sentence about who benefits and why it matters to every piece of work you hand over for the next month.

sparks.hook: Reviewing what happened, honestly, is worth more than any training course.
sparks.insight: The practice of stopping after a piece of work and reconstructing it together is one of the highest-return rituals a team can adopt, and it is almost always skipped for lack of time. It works when it is genuinely blameless and specific: what did we expect, what actually happened, why the gap, what changes. It stops working the moment somebody is punished for what they said in the room, because from then on people bring a version of events designed to survive the meeting.
sparks.why: Structured reflection converts experience into transferable knowledge, which otherwise stays inside individual heads. The blameless condition is not a nicety; it is what determines whether the accounts are true.
sparks.apply: Run a thirty-minute review after your next completed project, with four questions and an explicit rule that nobody's name goes in the notes.

carousel.title: Say what you expected
carousel.body: Start by reconstructing what the team believed would happen before it started. Without that baseline the discussion becomes a list of complaints rather than an analysis.

carousel.title: Say what actually happened
carousel.body: Establish the sequence of events factually before anybody interprets it. Disagreements about the facts are common and worth resolving first.

carousel.title: Work the gap
carousel.body: Ask why the two differ, and keep asking until you reach a mechanism rather than a person. If the answer is somebody's name, you have not finished.

carousel.title: Change one thing
carousel.body: End with a single specific change and an owner. A review that produces insight and no change trains people that the ritual is decorative.

sparks.hook: Add one sentence to your criticism and people act on it far more.
sparks.insight: There is a well-replicated finding in feedback research: attaching an explicit statement that you are giving these comments because the standard is high and you believe the person can reach it substantially raises the rate at which they revise their work. It sounds like a trick and it is not, because it has to be true. What it does is remove the ambiguity people otherwise resolve badly, deciding that the criticism means you have written them off. Naming your expectation closes that gap.
sparks.why: This comes from controlled studies of feedback framing and has replicated well. The mechanism is that criticism is ambiguous about intent, and the ambiguity is what triggers defensiveness rather than the content.
sparks.apply: Add one sentence to your next piece of critical feedback stating that you have high expectations and believe they can meet them.

sparks.hook: Where people sit and what you repeat weekly are your real culture policy.
sparks.insight: Culture is carried by mechanics far more than by intentions. Who sits near whom determines who talks. Which meeting recurs determines what gets attention. The ritual you repeat every week determines what people believe is normal. These are all things a manager can change directly, unlike attitudes, and they work whether or not anyone is paying attention. Most attempts at culture change fail because they target beliefs, which are downstream of the mechanics nobody bothered to alter.
sparks.why: Environment and routine shape behaviour continuously and without requiring anyone's agreement. That makes them more reliable levers than persuasion, which has to be repeated and can be resisted.
sparks.apply: Change one physical or scheduling arrangement this month — seating, a recurring meeting, a weekly ritual — and watch what shifts.

sparks.hook: Stories chosen from successful groups cannot tell you what caused the success.
sparks.insight: The method here is to study groups that already performed unusually well and look for what they had in common. That is an interesting way to generate ideas and a poor way to establish cause, because the unsuccessful groups doing the same things were never examined. Some of the underlying research is genuinely solid, particularly the work on safety and on feedback framing. Other chapters are vivid selections from organisations that were already winning. Read it for the practices and stay sceptical about the claim that they explain the results.
sparks.why: Selecting on the outcome makes almost any shared trait look causal. The safety and feedback research cited holds up independently; the case studies around it do not carry the same weight.
sparks.apply: Take two practices from this book, run them for a quarter, and measure something specific rather than assuming the effect transferred.

actions: Name one real mistake of your own in a team meeting this month, say what it cost, and attach no silver lining to it.
Run a blameless thirty-minute review after your next completed project, and finish with one specific change and a named owner.
Count speaking time in your next three meetings and directly invite the two quietest people into the conversation.
Change one scheduling or seating arrangement deliberately, then note what conversations start happening that were not happening before.
not_for_you_if: You want rigorous causal evidence rather than stories selected from groups that had already succeeded, or you dislike journalistic business writing.

verification.notes: First published January 2018 by Bantam. Journalistic synthesis of organisational research and case studies; the selection-on-success limitation is stated explicitly in the sparks.

title: Nine Lies About Work
subtitle: A Freethinking Leader's Guide to the Real World
author: Marcus Buckingham and Ashley Goodall
why_it_matters: It attacks the standard human-resources apparatus — cascaded goals, competency models, potential ratings, peer scoring — with an argument that most of it measures the rater rather than the person. Uncomfortable reading for anyone who runs a performance cycle.

crux.headline: Most people systems measure the rater, not the person
crux.body: Companies run on measurements that feel objective and are not. Ratings of another person's skills tell you far more about the person doing the rating than about the person being rated, and that is a measured effect rather than an opinion. Once you accept it, a lot of expensive machinery stops making sense: potential scores, competency grids, calibrated rankings. What survives is much smaller and more local — frequent attention from a team leader who actually watches the work.

sparks.hook: When you rate a colleague, most of what you record is you.
sparks.insight: Research on performance ratings consistently finds that the largest share of variance in a score reflects the idiosyncrasies of the person giving it: their own standards, their interpretation of the scale, their tendencies to be generous or severe. A much smaller share reflects the person being rated. This is not a claim about bad managers; it happens with trained, well-meaning raters. It means that averaging several people's ratings does not clean the noise, and the resulting number carries far less signal than the process implies.
sparks.why: The rater effect is one of the better-established findings in this area and has been replicated across settings. It undermines any system that treats a composite human rating as objective measurement.
sparks.apply: Stop averaging ratings of a person's abilities. Instead ask each manager what they would personally do with that person, which is a question they can answer.

sparks.hook: People do not join a company. They join whoever runs their team.
sparks.insight: Company-level culture surveys produce a single number for an organisation where the actual experience varies enormously between teams sitting twenty metres apart. What predicts whether somebody is engaged, stays, or does good work is almost entirely local: their immediate leader, their colleagues, whether the work makes sense. Company-wide programmes designed to fix an average therefore aim at something no employee experiences. The variation between teams inside a company is usually larger than the variation between companies.
sparks.why: The evidence here comes largely from the authors' own proprietary survey work, so treat the exact figures cautiously. The general finding that team-level variation dominates is consistent with other engagement research.
sparks.apply: Break your next engagement survey down by team rather than by company or division, and act only at the team level.

sparks.hook: Cascading goals downward mostly produces goals nobody can act on.
sparks.insight: The standard practice takes a company objective and divides it into departmental objectives, then into individual ones, on the assumption that alignment is arithmetic. What arrives at the bottom is usually a target somebody cannot influence, expressed in language borrowed from two levels up. What people actually need is the opposite direction of travel: enough understanding of what the organisation is for that they can invent sensible goals themselves. Meaning cascades usefully. Numbers mostly do not.
sparks.why: The critique is argument rather than measurement. It holds up best where individual contribution to a top-level number is genuinely untraceable, which describes most knowledge work.
sparks.apply: Replace one cascaded target this quarter with a short written explanation of what the organisation is trying to achieve and why.

sparks.hook: The best people are not well-rounded. They are lopsided and know it.
sparks.insight: Competency models describe an ideal person who is uniformly good at everything, and then measure real people against the gap. Excellent performers almost never look like that. They are unusually strong in a narrow band and unremarkable elsewhere, and their careers work because they built around the spike rather than filling in the dips. Development plans aimed at weaknesses produce slightly less bad performance in areas the person will never be good at, at the cost of the time that would have compounded the strength.
sparks.why: The argument is strongest where roles can be shaped around people. Where a role has genuine minimum requirements, a disqualifying weakness still has to be addressed rather than routed around.
sparks.apply: Rewrite one person's development plan so at least two of three goals build an existing strength rather than repairing a weakness.

sparks.hook: People do not need feedback nearly as much as they need attention.
sparks.insight: The word feedback has come to mean telling somebody what is wrong with them, and organisations have industrialised it. What actually improves performance is far more specific: someone watching your work closely enough to notice a moment when it went well, and telling you exactly what they saw. That is information you can use, because it identifies something real to repeat. Corrective feedback is still necessary for genuine failures, but it is a fraction of what most performance systems spend their time producing.
sparks.why: Attention to what worked gives a person a reproducible target, whereas correction only removes an error. The claim is argued rather than measured, and it does not license avoiding hard conversations.
sparks.apply: Catch each person doing one specific thing well this week and describe exactly what you saw within a day of seeing it.

carousel.title: Watch the actual work
carousel.body: You cannot notice a good moment you were not present for. Spend time close enough to the work that you have something specific to report back.

carousel.title: Describe, do not evaluate
carousel.body: Say precisely what they did and the effect it had, rather than assigning a grade. Description gives them something reproducible; a score gives them nothing to repeat.

carousel.title: Say it immediately
carousel.body: Within a day, ideally within the hour. Stored-up recognition delivered at a review has been stripped of the detail that made it useful in the first place.

carousel.title: Keep the hard ones separate
carousel.body: This does not replace addressing real problems. Keep corrective conversations distinct so that recognition never arrives with a warning attached to it.

sparks.hook: Potential is a label. Momentum is something you can actually observe.
sparks.insight: Organisations sort people into those who have potential and those who do not, then allocate opportunity accordingly, which makes the label self-fulfilling. The judgement is usually made early, on thin evidence, by someone whose own preferences shape it. A more honest question is about momentum: what is this person learning right now, how fast, and what are they doing with it. Momentum is visible, it changes, and it does not permanently sort people into categories on the basis of one manager's impression in year two.
sparks.why: Potential ratings are made by the same raters affected by the idiosyncrasy problem, then used to allocate opportunity, which makes the original judgement look accurate later.
sparks.apply: Remove potential ratings from your next talent review and discuss what each person has visibly learned in the last six months instead.

sparks.hook: Balance is the wrong target. Find the parts of the job you love, and grow them.
sparks.insight: Work-life balance treats work as uniformly draining and life as the only source of energy, which does not match how anyone actually experiences a job. Within any role there are activities that leave you energised and others that flatten you, and the ratio matters more than the hours. People who report a meaningful share of the week spent on work they genuinely like are more resilient and stay longer. The practical move is not fewer hours; it is changing the composition of them.
sparks.why: Drawn largely from the authors' own survey work, so the specific figures deserve caution. The underlying idea that activity composition matters more than raw hours is well supported in the burnout literature.
sparks.apply: Ask each person which parts of their week energise them, and change one thing so they get more of it next month.

sparks.hook: There is no list of leadership qualities. There are only people who follow.
sparks.insight: The search for the traits shared by great leaders has run for a century and produced lists that contradict each other, because the leaders studied genuinely have little in common. What they do share is an observable outcome: other people choose to follow them. That shifts the question from what qualities you should acquire to what you actually give people that makes following you worthwhile — usually confidence about the future and confidence that you are on their side.
sparks.why: Trait-based leadership research has a long record of weak and inconsistent findings. Defining leadership by the presence of followers is more measurable, though it says less about how to become one.
sparks.apply: Ask two people who follow you what specifically makes them do so, and stop trying to acquire traits that did not come up.

sparks.hook: A short weekly conversation about this week beats any annual process.
sparks.insight: The single practice most consistently associated with better team outcomes is unglamorous: a brief check-in every week, led by the immediate manager, about what the person is working on right now and what they need. Not a review, not a rating, not a form. The frequency is what does the work, because a conversation about next week can still change something, whereas a conversation about last year can only record. The cost is fifteen minutes per person and the discipline to never skip it.
sparks.why: The supporting data comes from the authors' own research, so treat the effect size cautiously. The mechanism — frequent, near-term, forward-looking attention — is consistent with the wider evidence on feedback timing.
sparks.apply: Start a fifteen-minute weekly check-in with each report about the coming week, and protect it more strictly than any other meeting.

carousel.title: Make it weekly and short
carousel.body: Fifteen minutes, every week, same slot. Frequency matters more than depth, and a long monthly session does not substitute for four short ones.

carousel.title: Ask about the coming week
carousel.body: Two questions: what are your priorities, and where do you need help. Looking forward means the conversation can still change the outcome it discusses.

carousel.title: Respond before the next one
carousel.body: Whatever they said they needed, do something about it within the week. A check-in that never produces action degrades into a status report within a month.

carousel.title: Never cancel it
carousel.body: Reschedule rather than skip. The reliability is most of the value, and the first cancellation tells people where the meeting sits in your real priorities.

sparks.hook: Attacking a bad measurement is easier than replacing it.
sparks.insight: The critique of standard performance machinery is largely sound, and the replacements offered are thinner than the demolition. Some of the evidence is proprietary survey work from the authors' own institute, which cannot be independently checked. And large organisations do need some way to distribute pay and promotion that is defensible to the people who did not get either. Take the rater-effect finding seriously, because it is solid. Be more careful before dismantling a process without a workable answer to what replaces it.
sparks.why: The rating research is well replicated and genuinely damaging to standard practice. The alternatives rest more on the authors' own data and on argument, which is a weaker footing than the critique they built.
sparks.apply: Fix the single worst-evidenced part of your performance process this year rather than replacing the whole thing at once.

actions: Start a fifteen-minute weekly check-in with every report about the coming week, and reschedule rather than cancel it.
Break your next engagement survey down to team level, and act only where a specific team's numbers say something.
Rewrite one person's development plan so most of it builds an existing strength rather than repairing a weakness.
Remove potential ratings from your next talent review and discuss visible learning over the last six months instead.
not_for_you_if: You need a working replacement for your performance process, or you dislike arguments built substantially on the authors' own unpublished survey data.

verification.notes: First published April 2019 by Harvard Business Review Press. The rater-effect research cited is independently established; much of the remaining evidence is the authors' own proprietary survey work, flagged in the sparks.
